title: Swim in Rising Water
pattern: Dijkstra on a grid: minimise the highest cell on the path
statement: `grid[r][c]` is the elevation of each cell of an `n × n` grid. At time `t` the water level is `t`, and you can swim between neighbouring cells only if **both** are at elevation `≤ t`. Swimming takes no time. Return the earliest time at which you can get from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell.

example.why: The path 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 along the top and right edge never climbs above 4; every other route passes a higher cell.

idea: A path is usable as soon as the water covers its **highest** cell. So we want the path from the top-left to the bottom-right whose highest cell is as low as possible.
Explore like Dijkstra: keep all reachable-but-unexplored cells in a min-heap, keyed by the water level needed to get there = the highest cell on the way.
Always expand the cell that needs the **lowest** level. When the bottom-right cell is popped, no cheaper way to it can exist — its level is the answer.

complexity.timeWhy: Each of the n² cells is pushed and popped at most once, at O(log n²) each.
complexity.spaceWhy: The visited set and the heap.

steps.text: Our example: **`grid = [[0,1,2],[5,8,3],[7,6,4]]`**. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
Start in the top-left cell. A heap entry is (water level needed to reach the cell, row, col); standing on the start already needs level 0.
